# Brief: scope the transcription of the parish ledgers before we take the grant

The heritage trust has offered to fund transcription of the parish ledgers, and
the offer has a deadline on it. Before we accept I want to know what we are
actually committing to, because the last time we took project money for a
collection we underestimated the work by a factor of three and finished it out
of our own reserves.

## What the collection is

Forty-one bound volumes covering 1798 to 1926, plus a box of loose sheets that
somebody at some point decided belonged with them. The bindings are mostly
sound. The ink is iron gall and has bled through on perhaps a fifth of the
pages, which is legible to a reader who is used to it and defeats every piece of
software we have tried.

The volumes are a ledger in the strict sense — dated entries, a sum, a name, and
frequently a marginal note in a second hand added years later. The marginal
notes are the part researchers actually want, and they are the part least
suited to any automated approach.

## The questions

- How many pages are there, really. The volumes are catalogued by year rather
  than by extent, and nobody has counted. A sample of eight volumes and an
  average would be enough to write a credible plan.
- What a page costs to transcribe, at the standard the trust expects, by a
  volunteer with the training we can realistically provide. I would rather know
  this from a trial of twenty pages than from a rate quoted in somebody else's
  project report.
- Whether the marginal notes are in scope. If they are, the reconciliation of a
  note against the entry it refers to is its own task and needs a convention
  before anybody starts, or we will get forty-one volumes transcribed to forty-
  one different standards.
- What we do about the loose sheets. My instinct is to exclude them from this
  piece of work and say so in the application, rather than discovering in month
  seven that they are a collection of their own.

## Constraints

The trust's money has to be spent within eighteen months and cannot be spent on
staff we already employ. Our volunteers are keen, mostly retired, and available
in quantities that vary sharply with the weather and the time of year. The
reading room cannot lose more than one table to the project during opening
hours.

## What I want back

A scope note the committee can vote on: pages, hours, a defensible cost, the
convention for the marginal notes, and an explicit list of what we are not
doing. If the honest conclusion is that the grant is too small for the
collection, say so — turning it down with a reason is a better outcome than
accepting it and finishing at our own expense again.
